posts.text:
I'm building Brad Devices, a computer company in Kisumu, Kenya. The rule is
software before silicon, receipts after that.

The receipt I want to show first is a compiler.

It compiles a C subset to BradISA V2, my own 32-bit instruction set. A small
emulator then runs the emitted code inside the test suite. Not "it assembles."
It executes.

add(3, 4) returns 7.
sum(10) returns 45.
An eight-argument function returns 36.
All 24 tests are green.

The language is deliberately small: int and void, functions, locals, if/else,
while, globals, arrays, pointers, int-field structs. No optimizer, no C++. It
exists to prove the ISA can be compiled at all — the part that was honestly
missing.

The live workbench: https://lnkd.in/dJENjwBV

#BradDevices #Compilers

posts.text:
I'm building Brad Devices, a computer company in Kisumu, Kenya. The rule is
software before silicon, receipts after that.

This receipt is a letter.

I drew the B. A shaded one, three ways: braille, blocks, and a density ramp.
The braille version is 55 columns wide and 19 rows tall.

It is not a picture of a logo. It is the logo, as characters.

Then it went to work.

- One file in the repository is the source. A script publishes it to every
  consumer: the CLI, the website's live terminal, and a public download.
- The CLI prints it only on an interactive terminal. Piped output and CI logs
  stay clean, because a banner in a log is noise everyone scrolls past.
- A gate refuses a mark that drifts from its source, grows past 80 columns, or
  that a command stops wearing.
- The website prints it at boot — and hides it from screen readers, because a
  picture of a letter is not a letter.

The whole point is that a mark living in one file cannot rot everywhere it
was copied.

Same discipline as the compiler. One source. Everything generated. A gate that
refuses.

The live workbench: https://lnkd.in/dYZHjsMJ

#BradDevices #Design
